overview: This three-page consular despatch reports senior personnel changes in Japan’s colonial Government-General of Taiwan following the Seiyūkai cabinet’s accession to power in December 1931. It describes the resignation of Governor-General Masahiro Ohta, the appointment and background of Hiroshi Minami, the replacement of Director-General Kinoshita by Hiroyoshi Hiratsuka, and changes in the leadership of the Japanese forces stationed in Taiwan. The report also comments on Taiwan’s strategic and commercial importance to Japan, its economic connections with South China and the South Seas, military censorship of the civilian administration, and the prospect of further bureaucratic changes under the incoming governor-general.

subfiles.title: Despatch from Ketcham on personnel changes in the Taiwan Government-General
subfiles.from: John B. Ketcham, American Consul at Taihoku
subfiles.about: Reports changes in the senior civil and military leadership of colonial Taiwan following the formation of the Seiyūkai cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Ketcham reports that Governor-General Masahiro Ohta resigned and was replaced by Hiroshi Minami, whose education, official career, family circumstances, and association with Prince Saionji are outlined. He also describes the retirement of Director-General Kinoshita and the arrival of Hiroyoshi Hiratsuka, who emphasized Taiwan’s strategic position and commercial relations with South China, the Philippines, and Malaysia. Finally, the despatch records the promotion of General Masaki, his replacement by General Abe, the military’s censorship of information from the civilian administration, and expectations of further changes among government bureau chiefs.

interest: The despatch provides a compact snapshot of the interaction between party politics in metropolitan Japan and administrative change in colonial Taiwan. Its biographical sketches reveal the career networks from which senior colonial officials were recruited, particularly Minami’s connection with Prince Saionji. Especially useful are Ketcham’s observations about the military’s censorship of the civilian government and Hiratsuka’s explicit conception of Taiwan as a commercial base for Japanese expansion toward South China and Southeast Asia.
